text: Doug Aitken, born in 1968 in Redondo Beach, California, is an American multidisciplinary artist whose body of work spans photography, print media, sculpture, architectural interventions, narrative films, sound, single and multi-channel video works, installations, and live performance. He studied magazine illustration with Philip Hays at the Art Center College of Design in Pasadena before graduating in Fine Arts in 1991. In 1994, he moved to New York, where he held his first solo show at 303 Gallery. Aitken's video works have been presented in culturally significant locations such as Jonestown in Guyana, southwest Africa's diamond mines, and India's Bollywood. He has created numerous site-specific installations that often integrate interactive media with architecture. A recent work, New Horizon, featured a reflective hot air balloon and gondola that transformed into a kinetic light sculpture and took place in July 2019 across Massachusetts. Another project, Underwater Pavilions (2016), consisted of three temporary sculptures moored to the ocean floor off Catalina Island, CA, designed to reflect and refract light, creating a portal that connected viewers to the ocean while disrupting conventional views of aquatic environments. The sculptures, developed in partnership with Parley for the Oceans and the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, featured mirrored sections that activated into kaleidoscopic observatories and responded to ocean currents and time of day, emphasizing the fluidity of time and space. The project also included a mirrored hexagonal room installation titled NEW ERA, shown in locations including New York, Zurich, Denmark, Beijing, California, and London, which mapped the development of the cellular telephone. In 2023, Aitken exhibited a five-channel video installation titled HOWL in Zürich, depicting oil derricks in a desolate California valley with soundbites from residents discussing the area’s oil-boom history and future. In 2000, the exhibition glass horizon featured a projection of "secession eyes" onto the Vienna Secession building, highlighting his interest in architecture and urban interaction. In 2001, Aitken transformed the Serpentine Gallery in London into a functional lighthouse for his installation New Ocean. In 2004, he co-curated Hard Light at MoMA PS1 with Klaus Biesenbach. In 2007, his installation Sleepwalkers, curated by Biesenbach and Creative Time, was presented at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, featuring eight projections on the museum’s exterior walls and a live happening with performers including Donald Sutherland, Tilda Swinton, Seu Jorge, and Cat Power. In 2008, Aitken created Migration for the 55th Carnegie International in Pittsburgh, part of a three-part trilogy entitled Empire, depicting migratory animals in empty hotel rooms. In 2012, he produced SONG 1 at the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, projecting a deconstructed version of the song "I Only Have Eyes for You" onto the convex exterior of the building, requiring viewers to move around it to see the full experience. ALTERED EARTH (2012) explored the Camargue region of southern France using a maze-like arrangement of twelve large projections in Arles’ Grande Halle, inspiring an app for the Apple iPad. In 2013, Mirror, a large LED screen wrapped around the Seattle Art Museum, used a computer program to select footage from central Seattle and surrounding areas based on live data such as weather and traffic. Aitken has directed live "happenings," including Broken Screen events in Los Angeles and New York (2006), and in 2009 staged a real-time opera titled "the handle comes up, the hammer comes down" at Theater Basel, featuring auctioneers performing against the rhythms of his Sonic Table. In 2009, he presented Frontier on the Tiber River in Rome and staged a happening with the same title, featuring Ed Ruscha in a fictional landscape. Black Mirror, shown first at the Deste Foundation in Hydra and later on a custom barge, used five screens reflected into infinity and included performers such as Chloë Sevigny, Leo Gallo, and Tim McAfee-Lewis. Aitken is known for photographs that explore spatial and temporal disruption, such as Passenger (1999), which shows planes in flight over desolate airport landscapes. He has also created aluminum light boxes combining photographic images and text, and sculptures made from plants in clear acrylic and kaleidoscopic mirrors, as well as hand-carved foam, epoxy, and hand silk-screened acrylic. His scores include field recordings such as jungle sounds from Jonestown, Guyana (1995 monsoon), and volcanic tremors from Montserrat (1998 eraser). In 1996, he created an installation in the Brooklyn Bridge’s Anchorage using traffic noise recordings. In 2004, he completed a sound sculpture for the Barcelona Pavilion with rotating steel branches and directional speakers playing scripted conversations. In 2009, the Sonic Pavilion opened in Brazil’s Inhotim, where sounds from deep underground were amplified through speakers. Aitken has collaborated with musicians including André 3000, Lichens, and No Age on film scores. He has produced several books, including I AM A BULLET (2000), Doug Aitken: A-Z Book (2003), Broken Screen (2005), Sleepwalkers (2007), 99 Cent Dreams (2008), Write In Jerry Brown President (2008), The Idea of the West (2010), Black Mirror (2011), and SONG 1 (2012), with some tied to exhibitions or happenings. Two comprehensive monographs on his career are Doug Aitken: 100 YRS (Rizzoli) and Doug Aitken: Electric Earth (Prestel). Station to Station, a nomadic "Happening" launched in fall 2013, traveled from New York City to San Francisco, making nine stops in cities including Pittsburgh, Chicago, Minneapolis/St. Paul, Santa Fe, Winslow, Arizona, Barstow, California, and Oakland. Supported by institutions such as MoMA PS1, Carnegie Museum of Art, MCA Chicago, Walker Art Center, SITE Santa Fe, LACMA, and SFMOMA, the project served as a cultural incubator, featuring artists like Kenneth Anger, Olafur Eliasson, and Nam June Paik, musicians including Beck, Cat Power, and The Black Monks of Mississippi, and contributors such as Taylor-Ruth Baldwin, Catherine Opie, and Raymond Pettibon. All proceeds from the project funded multi-museum arts programs in 2014.

From June 27 to July 26, 2015, Doug Aitken staged Station to Station: A 30 Day Happening at the Barbican Centre in London, envisioning it as a living exhibition where the entire multi-arts facility was transformed into a large-scale, multi-disciplinary event involving more than 100 artists, including Olafur Eliasson, Martin Creed, and Terry Riley. The event featured artists such as Meschac Gaba, Liz Glynn, Fischli & Weiss, Fritz Haeg, Carsten Höller, Ernesto Neto, Nam June Paik, Jorge Pardo, Jack Pierson, Nicolas Provost, Stephen Shore, Rirkrit Tiravanija, and Lawrence Weiner, as well as musicians like Beck, The Black Monks of Mississippi, Boredoms, Jackson Browne, Cat Power, Cold Cave, The Congos, Dan Deacon, Eleanor Friedberger, The Handsome Family, Lia Ices, Kansas City Marching Cobras, Lucky Dragons, Thurston Moore, Giorgio Moroder, Nite Jewel, No Age, Patti Smith, Ariel Pink’s Haunted Graffiti, Savages (band), Mavis Staples, Suicide (band), Sun Araw, Thee Satisfaction, Twin Shadow, and others. Printed matter contributors included Taylor-Ruth Baldwin, Yto Barrada, Sam Durant, Karen Kilimnik, Urs Fischer, Catherine Opie, Jack Pierson, Raymond Pettibon, and Josh Smith. Food was provided by Alice Waters and the Edible Schoolyard Project and chef Leif Hedendal. On August 21, 2015, a feature film directed by Aitken, using footage from the 2013 happenings, titled Station to Station, premiered in Los Angeles. Described as "...a textured, visceral collection of 62 shorts capturing moments during the three-week journey...", the film was experimental in format. Doug Aitken has participated in over 200 art exhibitions worldwide, with works featured in group exhibitions at institutions such as the Whitney Museum of American Art, The Museum of Modern Art, and the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris. He has had solo exhibitions at the Schirn Kunsthalle, Frankfurt, the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, the Serpentine Gallery, London, Kunsthalle Zürich, Switzerland, Kunsthaus Bregenz, Austria, Museum of Modern Art, New York, Deste Foundation, Greece, and Tokyo Opera City Art Gallery, Japan. In 2006, the Aspen Art Museum held the first exhibition dedicated solely to Aitken's photography. From September 10, 2016, to January 15, 2017, The Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, at the Geffen Contemporary, presented Doug Aitken: Electric Earth, the artist's first North American mid-career survey, which traveled to The Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth, TX, from May 28, 2017, to August 20, 2017. Aitken is represented by 303 Gallery, New York; Regen Projects, Los Angeles; Galerie Eva Presenhuber, Zürich; and Victoria Miro Gallery, London. Grosenick, Uta; Riemschneider, Burkhard, eds. (2005).
